meaning: The number of men registered from the tribe of Gad in the first census in the wilderness
description: The number 45650 is given in Numbers 1:25 and 2:15 as the count of fighting men from the tribe of Gad, counted during the first census in the wilderness of Sinai. The muster was carried out by the Lord's command, where all men from twenty years old and upward who could go to war were registered tribe by tribe. The tribe of Gad was placed in the camp south of the tabernacle, under the banner of Reuben, together with the tribes of Reuben and Simeon. This arrangement shows that Israel's army was not only a military organization but a theocratic community where God's presence in the tabernacle was central. At the second census, described in Numbers 26:18, the tribe of Gad had fallen to 40500 registered men – a decrease of 5150, which may reflect the trials and judgments that struck the people during their wilderness journey.

footnotes.text: Gad was the son of Jacob and Zilpah, Leah's maidservant (Gen 30:10–11). The name Gad means "fortune" or "troop," and Jacob's blessing over Gad in Gen 49:19 reads: "Gad – a troop shall press upon him, but he shall press upon their heels." This was understood as a prophecy about the tribe's warrior character.

The tribe of Gad later chose to settle east of the Jordan (Num 32), an area well suited for livestock. Moses gave them permission on the condition that their fighting men crossed the Jordan and fought alongside the other tribes before returning.

The decline from 45650 to 40500 between the two censuses may be linked to events such as the rebellion at Baal-Peor (Num 25) and other judgments in the wilderness, although the text does not specify which tribes were hardest hit.
